summary: For children aged 5-6, attending to precision means using mathematical words carefully: comparison words ('more than / fewer than / the same as'), shape vocabulary ('sides', 'corners', shape names), and positional words (above, below, behind, next to). A key proposed teaching move is to make vague language have a visible consequence so the child can discover the value of a precise word — a research-informed approach rather than a uniquely required method — following an informal→formal journey that starts from the child's own words ('pointy', 'big') and helps them rephrase ('has points', 'taller'). Children also need exposure to a WIDE VARIETY of examples of each shape so they do not form a narrow, prototype-bound concept.
misconceptions: Uses ambiguous everyday words where a precise one exists — 'big' for tall or for 'more', 'by' for a specific position (EEF)
Recognises only prototype shapes — rejects a long or upside-down triangle as 'not a triangle', calls a tilted square a 'diamond' (EEF: needs varied exposure)
Uses 'sides' and 'corners' interchangeably, or counts corners when asked for sides
Thinks a shape's name depends on how it is turned or how big it is, rather than its properties

activities.title: Tell the literal robot where teddy goes
steps: Direct a friendly robot (or puppet/character) to place teddy somewhere, e.g. say 'put teddy by the box'.

Watch the robot do EXACTLY what the words say — 'by the box' only means near the box, so the robot might put teddy behind it, in front of it, or beside it — so the ambiguity can produce a result that is not where the child meant.
Refine the instruction to a precise positional word ('on top of the box', 'behind the box') and check the robot now gets it right.
Repeat with a comparison round: ask for 'the tower with MORE blocks' rather than 'the bigger tower', to distinguish taller from more.
Say, in the child's own words, why the exact word helped the robot understand.
activities.insight: A vague everyday word (like 'by' or 'big') often fails to pin down the meaning; choosing a precise word (on top of / behind; taller / more) lets a listener do exactly what you intend.

activities.title: A character who takes your words literally
steps: Talk with a playful character (puppet or robot friend) who cheerfully misunderstands vague instructions, e.g. 'You said BY the box, so I put teddy BEHIND it — right?'
Answer the character's clarifying questions to pin down the position, comparison, or shape word you meant.
Keep each exchange short, and restate the instruction precisely until the character gets it right.
activities.insight: Being asked 'did you mean this or that?' makes a child notice an ambiguity and reach for the word that removes it — the repair IS the practice.

activities.title: The varied shape gallery (sides, corners and non-prototypes)
steps: Explore a gallery of many triangles and quadrilaterals shown in varied orientations and sizes — long thin triangles, upside-down triangles, tilted squares.
Trace a finger along each SIDE and point to each CORNER as they are named, then reveal the shape's name.

Decide whether a tilted square is still a square (it has four equal sides and four square corners, however it is turned) and whether a long or upside-down triangle is still a triangle (it is a closed shape with three straight sides).
Sort a tilted square into the 'square' group by its properties rather than by how it looks or how it is turned.
activities.insight: A shape's name depends on its properties (its straight sides and its corners), not on its size or orientation; 'side' and 'corner' name different features.

activities.title: Place the object in a spatial scene
steps: Place teddy in a scene above, below, behind, or next to another object, choosing the positional word that matches where you want it.
Describe aloud where you put teddy using the precise positional word.
Swap roles: a partner states a position and you place teddy to match, then check it agrees.
activities.insight: Positional language describes genuine spatial relationships; the right word lets another person find the object exactly.

checkQuestion: I'm going to tell you where teddy is: 'teddy is by the box.' Does that tell you EXACTLY where to find teddy, or could teddy be in lots of different places? Show me. How would you say it so I know exactly where teddy is?
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child noticing that 'by' is vague (teddy could be on top, behind, beside, inside) and reaching for a precise positional word, and ideally saying why it matters (so the listener isn't confused). This is surfaced for discussion, not marked right or wrong.
